newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Foreigners buy S.Korean blue chips under new limit.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners buy S.Korean blue chips under new limit.

text.p: Foreign investors focussed their buying on South Korean blue chip shares on Friday, the first day of the latest increase in the ceiling on foreign-owned stocks, as domestic institutions fed their demand, brokers said.
The ceiling, which rose to 23 percent from 20 percent, is applied to foreign holdings in individual companies.

Brokers said a familiar pattern emerged with domestic institutional investors profiting from sales of their blue-chip holdings to foreign investors eager to avoid the usual premiums of the over-the-counter market.
"It's a typical pattern that local institutions sell and foreigners try to accumulate their favourites on the first day of the ceiling expansion," said Park Key-pyong of Hanyang Securities.
Provisional figures from the Securities Supervisory Board showed foreign investors bought a net 611.6 billion won ($685.5 million) worth of Korean stocks.
An official at the Korea Stock Exchange said a total of 42 shares had sold out to foreigners, including SK Telecom, POSCO and Kookmin Bank.
The bourse list included some shares with less than one percent of shares remaining under the ceiling, including Samsung Electronics with 248 shares and Hyundai Motor with 267.
The 42 also included some stocks whose limit was reached before the expansion due to direct foreign investment or issuances of overseas equity-linked securities.

SK Telecom was the most preferred share in Friday's foreign buying. The bid to share ratio for the nation's largest cellular phone operator was 118. But Kookmin Bank topped today's foreign buying volume list with 4.18 million shares.

"Foreign buying orders in selective blue chips exceeded expectations," said Choi Bum of C.S. First Boston. "But domestic institutional investors dumped their holdings and tried to reshuffle their investment portfolios."
Heavy institutional selling pressured blue chips. SK Telecom fell 29,000 won, or 6.36 percent, to 427,000, and Hyundai Motor shed 1,100 won, or 4.68 percent, to 22,400.

But POSCO and Samsung Electronics recouped early falls in the belief they had been undervalued. The steelmaker added 400 won to 54,000 and the chipmaker rose 700 won to 61,300, contributing to the major index closing higher.
The composite stock index rose 2.87 points to 706.10.
Foreign buying was also strong for Sungmi Telecom and Samchully, which are not considered blue chips.
Del Ricks, head of research at BZW Securities, said some foreign investors were buying shares of smaller, non-blue chip companies under the new ceiling for convenience.

"There are these companies that are attracting interest just because of the opportunity to buy them without going to the over-the-counter market," Ricks said. "You could find them before but it might take a week to get what you wanted."
Some brokers had predicted that foreign investors would buy only blue chips because of concerns about corporate failures and Korea's poor economic fundamentals.

Brokers said cheap, large-capitalised shares came into the spotlight as domestic institutions were expected to switch their interest to those stocks after profiting from blue-chip sales to foreigners.
Choi said the market would head for the 750 level with buying centred on cheap large-cap shares. "But the index will lose about 100 points after that," he said.
